st.t: AI insurance: Coverage cannot replace professional governance
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s caution that an AI-insurance label does not establish comprehensive protection: Corgi’s offering is modular, subject to separate limits and retentions, and restricted to expressly selected modules. It does not independently establish claims performance, pricing maturity, or that coverage can substitute for professional governance.

It does not materially address the cluster’s broader claims about jagged capability, selective deployment or workflow redesign.

kp.k: AI liability insurance targets providers and business users
kp.d: The article reports that Corgi, a new Y Combinator-backed insurer that recently raised $108m, is offering AI liability insurance for AI companies and businesses using their tools, potentially including law firms. CEO Nico Laqua describes coverage as following liability on either side; the article does not establish that every law-firm use is covered.
qs: Corgi, a new insurance company backed by Y Combinator, is now offering AI liability insurance
Where the liability is, we cover
They’ve recently raised $108m.

kp.k: Modular coverage addresses multiple AI-specific risks
kp.d: Corgi's quoted AI and Algorithmic Liability Endorsement (CORG-TECH-0038) offers selected modules with separate limits and retentions. Listed risks include algorithmic bias, hallucination/defamation, training-data misuse, data poisoning/adversarial attacks, autonomous-AI bodily injury, deepfakes and synthetic media, service interruption, intellectual property, regulatory investigation defense and civil fines where insurable. Coverage is conditional on selecting the relevant modules, rather than blanket protection against AI failures.
qs: AI and Algorithmic Liability Endorsement (CORG-TECH-0038)
A modular endorsement for companies using AI, machine learning, or automated decision-making. You select the modules you need — each with its own limit and retention.
regulatory investigation defense, and civil fines (where insurable).
[Endorsement required — coverage applies only to selected modules].

kp.k: Professional liability coverage addresses alleged AI financial losses
kp.d: The article quotes Corgi's website describing Tech & AI Liability as professional liability insurance for AI companies, covering legal defense and damages when customers allege that failures caused financial loss. The stated categories are model performance and hallucination, algorithmic bias and training-data disputes. Tromans explicitly says its relationship to the modular endorsement is unclear.
qs: Tech & AI Liability is a specific evolution of professional liability insurance designed for artificial intelligence companies.
It covers legal defense and damages if a customer alleges that your AI model, software, or algorithm failed to perform as intended and caused them a financial loss.
Corgi explicitly covers three AI risk categories: model performance & hallucination, algorithmic bias, and training data disputes.
Although, it’s not clear if the immediately above connects to the policy AI and Algorithmic Liability Endorsement offering.

kp.k: Agent coverage is emerging, but offering remains uncertain
kp.d: Tromans reports that the announcement the day before publication mentioned insurance against agents going wrong. He characterizes Corgi's offering as rapidly evolving, while limiting his concrete policy discussion to what he could identify on its website at the time. This is reporting on an emerging offering, not confirmation of comprehensive agent coverage.
qs: It seems that what they offer is evolving rapidly
insuring against agents going wrong
Overall, it feels like Corgi’s offering is rapidly expanding and evolving as new AI aspects come to their attention.

kp.k: Insurance availability addresses reported legal-market demand
kp.d: Tromans considers the launch significant because some major insurers reportedly avoid AI coverage due to uncertainty about risks. As anecdotal evidence of demand, he cites recurring questions at his legal-AI talks about insuring tool outputs, alongside questions about training junior lawyers. He expects interest from law firms, in-house teams and legal technology companies, without offering systematic demand data.
qs: It’s been reported that some major insurance companies don’t want to get involved in AI-related coverage, in part because it’s such a new market space that they don’t know the risks, so want to avoid it.
but how will we train junior lawyers in the future?
can you insure against what these tools do?
So, this will be interesting to plenty of law firms, inhouse teams, and legal tech companies.

kp.k: Orbital provides a qualified legal-AI insurance precedent
kp.d: The author identifies Orbital's residential-property work as the only legal-AI example known to Artificial Lawyer of a company specifically offering insurance against its own outputs. This is explicitly a knowledge-qualified observation, not an exhaustive finding about the insurance market.
qs: As far as AL knows, there is only one legal AI company that specifically offers insurance against its own outputs, and that’s Orbital, in relation to residential property work.

kp.k: Corgi CEO endorses AI-native legal services
kp.d: Laqua expresses the opinion that law, alongside insurance, is an especially strong AI use case because of productivity gains, and reports that Corgi heavily uses AI-native law firms. These are the interviewee's assessments and reported purchasing behavior, not measured productivity findings.
qs: Besides insurance, legal is the best use case of AI, *IMO*. Lots of productivity gains. I’m very excited about everything I’m seeing there and we are heavy users of AI native law firms.

kp.k: Law-firm responsibility remains jurisdiction-dependent and potentially contested
kp.d: Tromans reports others' view that, depending on local rules, law firms bear total responsibility for anything sent to clients regardless of how it was produced. He speculates about whether that position might evolve as AI becomes pervasive in firm outputs, rather than identifying an actual rule change, and recommends consulting regulators and other experts.
qs: many have suggested that dependent on one’s local rules, anything a law firm sends to a client – no matter how it’s made – is the firm’s total responsibility.
But, who knows how this position will evolve as ‘legal AI’ becomes synonymous with the outputs of law firms in general?
But, again, talk to your regulators and other experts!

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Tromans reports that Corgi is offering AI liability insurance for AI providers and businesses using AI, potentially including law firms, and anticipates interest across the legal market.
pts.d: The article presents insurance as a response to risks arising from AI outputs and autonomous agents. Corgi CEO Nico Laqua describes the intended coverage broadly. The website materials reproduced in the article describe modular coverage for specified AI risks and defense and damages for alleged failures causing financial loss. Tromans does not establish that every listed risk or every law-firm use is covered.

pts.k: Laqua identifies legal work as an especially promising AI use case with substantial productivity gains.
pts.d: This is the interviewed CEO's explicitly personal assessment, accompanied by his statement that his company is a heavy user of AI-native law firms. The article provides no quantified productivity finding.

pts.k: Tromans characterizes AI insurance as an important emerging market where coverage uncertainty coincides with legal-sector demand.
pts.d: He reports that some major insurers avoid AI coverage because risks are unfamiliar, describes recurring insurance questions at his legal-AI talks, and identifies Orbital as the only legal-AI company known to him that specifically insures its own outputs, in residential property work. His Orbital statement is expressly limited to his knowledge, not presented as a comprehensive market census.

pts.k: Tromans raises the possibility that responsibility for law-firm outputs could evolve as legal AI becomes more pervasive, without predicting a specific legal change.
pts.d: He reports an unnamed view that firms remain fully responsible for client-facing work regardless of how it is produced, subject to local rules. He then questions how that position might evolve. This is an open question and speculative framing, not a finding that AI has already transferred responsibility away from firms.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of the CEO's statements, Corgi's published product descriptions, and Tromans's market knowledge and speaking experience.
pts.d: The coverage account draws on Laqua's response on X and website descriptions, including the AI and Algorithmic Liability Endorsement (CORG-TECH-0038). The productivity assessment is opinion supported only by reported experience using AI-native firms. Legal-sector interest is supported by the author's anecdotal experience of audience questions. Insurer reluctance is attributed to unspecified reports. No productivity data, claims-payment experience, actuarial analysis, or systematic insurance-market survey is supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The account concerns coverage available as of 5 May 2026, with rapidly evolving offerings and material limits on what is established.
pts.d: Tromans refers to an announcement from the preceding day and describes the offering as still expanding. The quoted endorsement applies only to selected modules, each with its own limit and retention; civil fines are included only where insurable. He explicitly cannot confirm how a separate Tech & AI Liability website description connects to the endorsement. Potential changes in law-firm responsibility have no specified date and depend on local rules.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are AI providers, business users, potentially law firms, in-house legal teams, legal-tech companies, and customers alleging AI-caused losses.
pts.d: AI providers and eligible users are presented as prospective insurance buyers. The website description addresses defense and damages when a customer alleges financial loss from an AI failure. Law firms and in-house teams are identified as interested audiences rather than confirmed insureds. Orbital's residential-property work is the specific legal segment cited as already having output insurance. AI-native law firms appear separately as providers Laqua says his company uses.
